title: Security Analytics For Managing Security Screening Across Multiple Locations at Once
summary: Security analytics help teams monitor screening activity, track alerts, identify trends, and improve security operations across locations.
body_markdown:
Installing a screening system is just the start. Once it’s running, you still need to[manage entrances](https://www.securityinfowatch.com/perimeter-security/threat-detection-imaging-inspection/article/55398926/beyond-the-checkpoint-security-screening-in-2026) , coordinate staff, keep visitors moving, and keep leadership updated. If you oversee more than one building or campus, that gets harder fast without security analytics.


#### Questions that come up:


- Are the systems online?


- Is screening a smooth experience for visitors?


- Is today busier or slower than usual?


- Have any alerts come up that need attention?


Most teams answer these questions with phone calls, check-ins, and emails. The problem is timing. Screening activity changes by the minute. By the time an update reaches the right person, the moment it describes has often passed.


## Who Needs Visibility Into Screening Operations?


A school district security director might be responsible for screening across multiple schools. A hospital security team might cover several entrances spread across one campus. A venue manager might need to confirm every system is ready before the crowds arrive. All three need the same thing: a clear picture of what’s happening, without having to stand at every entrance themselves.


## Why Is Remote Access to Alert Images Important?


When a system flags an alert, the operator standing next to it usually knows the most. Everyone else is working from a phone call or a guess. That’s why many security leaders want the ability to pull up alert images remotely, so their team can stay informed and provide support when needed.


This matters after the fact, too. If a team needs to look back at a specific incident, or pull records for an investigation, having alert images and event logs on hand makes that possible.


## What Happens When a Threat Is Identified During Screening?


When a staff member identifies and tags a threat, key personnel often need to know right away, including the security director, administrators, and operations leaders. Getting that notification out fast helps everyone stay coordinated, share what they know, and respond together instead of catching up later.


## Using Screening Data to Inform Security Decisions


Leadership teams usually want to know several things, including how many visitors came through, how many alerts occurred, what type of alerts they were, how heavily each system is being used, and whether any of that is trending up or down over time. That information feeds into staffing decisions, budget requests, and the reports leadership already has to produce. It’s also the clearest way to show how screening is performing over time, not just today.
